page: Microsoft Azure NC16as_T4_v3 is a specialized compute instance belonging to the NCas_T4_v3 family, configured to provide dedicated GPU acceleration on AMD hardware. Running on the x86_64 architecture under the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor, the virtual machine provides 16 dedicated vCPUs backed by 110 GB of system memory, resulting in an allocation of approximately 6.88 GB of RAM per vCPU.

Hardware acceleration is supplied by a single NVIDIA T4 GPU containing 16 GB of dedicated VRAM. The host instance includes 378 GB of local SSD storage, which functions as fast scratch space and operational cache. The system also supports Azure Premium Storage for persistent managed disk attachments, though complimentary public IPv4 addresses are not provided by default.

From an infrastructure efficiency perspective, the NC16as_T4_v3 represents an economical accelerator option compared to high-tier training clusters. The single-GPU design and 16 GB of accelerator memory do not target large foundation model training, but they provide balanced capacity for throughput-oriented tasks. Best-fit workloads include deep learning inference, video transcoding, image processing, interactive graphics workstations, and GPU-assisted simulation pipelines.
description: Microsoft Azure NC16as_T4_v3 is a GPU-accelerated virtual machine tailored for inference and graphics workloads within the NCas_T4_v3 series. Built on the x86_64 architecture with AMD processors, this instance allocates 16 dedicated vCPUs alongside 110 GB of system memory, providing approximately 6.88 GB of RAM per vCPU. Acceleration is delivered via a single NVIDIA T4 GPU equipped with 16 GB of VRAM. For caching and operational scratch space, the instance includes 378 GB of bundled local SSD storage. Microsoft Hyper-V serves as the underlying virtualization layer, and the configuration supports Premium Storage integration. Because the instance pairs a mid-tier accelerator with substantial host memory and 16 compute cores, it delivers balanced resource efficiency without the overhead of heavy training hardware. Primary workload targets include machine learning model inference, video transcoding, visual computing, rendering, and GPU-accelerated data processing.
